Neuenkamp
NOY-en-kahmp
n. (the Pomeranian Cistercian abbey of 1231, dissolved 1535, whose stones built the town of Franzburg)
German Neuenkamp, the new field, from neu and Kamp, an enclosed field.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Neuenkamp in western Pomerania was founded in 1231 from Hiddensee's mother house at Neuencamp and became a considerable landowner on the Barth peninsula, founding in turn the island house on Hiddensee. It was dissolved in 1535. Duke Bogislaw XIII then did something unusually frank: he built himself a residence from the abbey and laid out a new town beside it, named Franzburg after his father-in-law, using the conventual buildings as a quarry. The church went into the houses. The dictionary records Neuenkamp for the plainness of that transaction and for the question Scripture puts to every builder. Christ's own prophecy over the temple was that its stones would be taken apart, “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2), so a dismantled sanctuary is not outside the ways of God. But the Lord also requires a reckoning before the first stone is laid, “sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28), and the prophet rebukes exactly the order of priorities Bogislaw followed, a panelled house beside a ruined one, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). When men go silent, the material itself is said to be competent to testify, “the stones would immediately cry out” (Luk 19:40).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a quarry as a place where stones are dug; to demolish as to throw down a building; a residence as the place of abode; ceiled as having an inner roof or lining; and a cost as the price of a thing, the expense.

expand to see more

QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, or separated from a large mass of rocks.

DEMOLISH, v.t. To throw or pull down; to raze; to destroy; to ruin; applied chiefly to buildings.

RESIDENCE, n. The place of abode; a dwelling; a habitation.

CEILED, pp. Furnished with an inner roof or lining; overlaid with wainscot or plaster.

COST, n. The price, value or equivalent of a thing purchased; expense; charge.

Key Scripture

Mat 24:2 — "And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down."

Luk 14:28 — "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?"

Hag 1:4 — "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?"

Luk 19:40 — "And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out."

Modern Corruption

Pomeranian Cistercian house of 1231 dissolved in 1535 and quarried for the duke's residence and the new town of Franzburg.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that stones are not sacred and priorities are. Neuenkamp went into houses, and Christ had already said of a far holier building that its masonry would come apart, “See ye not all these things?” (Mat 24:2), so the dismantling by itself proves nothing either way.

The live temptation is the order Bogislaw chose, which is to finish one's own house first. The Lord requires a reckoning before building begins, “intending to build a tower” (Luk 14:28); Haggai names the sin precisely as panelling a private dwelling while God's house lies waste, “and this house lie waste” (Hag 1:4); and where men keep quiet about such things the material is said to be competent to speak, “if these should hold their peace” (Luk 19:40).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek lithos (G3037), a stone; Greek psephizo (G5585), to count up, to reckon; Hebrew saphan (H5603), to cover, to panel; Hebrew chareb (H2720), waste, desolate.

expand to see more

Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone, a building stone; “There shall not be left here one stone upon another”, Matthew 24:2.

Greek psephizo (G5585) — to count with pebbles, to reckon up; “counteth the cost”, Luke 14:28.

Greek purgos (G4444) — a tower; “intending to build a tower”, Luke 14:28.

Hebrew saphan (H5603) — to cover in, to panel, to ceil; “to dwell in your cieled houses”, Haggai 1:4.

Greek krazo (G2896) — to cry out, to shriek; “the stones would immediately cry out”, Luke 19:40.

Usage

"“There shall not be left here one stone upon another” (Mat 24:2) — stones are not the sacred thing."

"“and this house lie waste” (Hag 1:4) — the order of priorities Haggai rebukes."

"“counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28) — the reckoning required before building."
